These probabilities are estimates from general knowledge of NAS-Bench-201, not computed from the benchmark data. Priors were kept low because a claim needs a consistent interaction across all three datasets and a meaningful margin.

My reasoning drew on a few structural points:
- Edge 3 (0→3) is a direct path from input to output. Setting it to skip_connect helps most when the other paths are weak or absent, and helps less when they are strong.
- Edge 2 (1→2) is the middle edge. Setting it to none matters less when other paths such as edge 1 or edge 4 are strong convs.
- Edge 0 and edge 1 are the input edges. Their effects tend to be larger and depend on downstream convs.

| Claim | Probability | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 30 | Edge 0 as conv_1x1 gives a strong path, so skip on edge 3 adds less. |
| 1 | 35 | Removing edge 2 costs more if edge 4 is a conv; the sign is ambiguous. |
| 2 | 30 | Edge 1 as skip suggests an existing skip path. |
| 3 | 40 | Skip on edge 0 feeds a downstream conv on edge 2, so this is plausible. |
| 4 | 35 | Skip on edge 4 is weak against a strong conv on edge 5. |
